props.title: Syndromes and a Century
props.initialSlug: A healing odyssey unlike any other.

sections.content: Syndromes and a Century (2006) represents Thai director Apichatpong Weerasethakul's most structurally ambitious work, splitting its narrative into two mirrored halves that reflect his parents' lives as doctors. Like Last Year at Marienbad (1961), it plays with time and memory in a hypnotic way. The film's architectural spaces - from rural clinics to sterile urban hospitals - become characters themselves, similar to how Tarkovsky used locations in Stalker (1979). Weerasethakul's signature dreamlike pacing and ethereal atmosphere influenced later works like Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives (2010).

sections.content: The film's innovative structure deeply influenced contemporary slow cinema. Its first half, set in a rural clinic, carries a warm nostalgia while the second half in Bangkok's modern hospital creates deliberate emotional distance. This mirroring technique was later echoed in films like Certified Copy (2010) and The Double Life of Véronique (1991). Weerasethakul's treatment of time as fluid rather than linear opened new possibilities for narrative cinema.

The film's handling of memory and place connects to a broader tradition of Asian art cinema, from Taiwanese director Tsai Ming-liang's What Time Is It There? (2001) to Hong Sang-soo's Right Now, Wrong Then (2015). Yet Weerasethakul's distinct Thai Buddhist perspective gives the film a unique metaphysical quality, where past and present, rural and urban, traditional and modern exist simultaneously. movies.title: Blissfully Yours
movies.slug: Weerasethakul's breakthrough film about forbidden love and escape into nature

sections.content: Syndromes and a Century helped establish a new visual language for depicting memory and time in cinema. Its influence can be seen in works like Lav Diaz's Evolution of a Filipino Family (2004) and Carlos Reygadas' Silent Light (2007). The film's bold formal experimentation with structure, duration, and parallel narratives opened new possibilities for art cinema in the 21st century.

The film's exploration of medical spaces as sites of both healing and alienation resonates with later works like The Death of Mr. Lazarescu (2005) and The Diving Bell and the Butterfly (2007). Weerasethakul's ability to find poetry in institutional settings influenced filmmakers like Pedro Costa in Horse Money (2014) and Lucien Castaing-Taylor in Leviathan (2012).
